# 2 Kings Chapter 17 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 237v–239r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_017_page_473.jpg, 2KI_017_page_474.jpg, 2KI_017_page_475.jpg, 2KI_017_page_476.jpg

---

**1** In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king of Israel in Samaria. He reigned for nine years.

**2** He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, though not to the extent of the Israelite kings before him.

**3** King Shalmaneser of Assyria attacked him, and Hoshea submitted, becoming his vassal and paying tribute.

**4** But the Assyrian king discovered that Hoshea was plotting against him — he had sent secret envoys to King So of Egypt and had stopped paying his annual tribute. So the king of Assyria had him arrested and thrown in prison.

**5** Then the Assyrian king invaded the whole country, marched on Samaria, and laid siege to it for three years.

**6** In Hoshea's ninth year, the king of Assyria finally captured Samaria. He deported the Israelites to Assyria and resettled them in Halah, along the Habor River in the region of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.

**7** All of this happened because the Israelites had sinned against the LORD their God, who had rescued them from Egypt, from the power of Pharaoh. They had worshiped other gods instead,

**8** adopting the practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before them, as well as the practices introduced by the kings of Israel.

**9** The Israelites did things in secret that offended the LORD their God. They built pagan shrines in every town, from the smallest outpost to the largest fortress.

**10** They set up sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every hilltop and under every leafy tree.

**11** At every one of these shrines they burned incense, just as the nations before them had done — the very nations the LORD had exiled. They did wicked things that provoked the LORD's anger.

**12** They worshiped worthless idols, even though the LORD had specifically told them, "You must not do this."

**13** Again and again the LORD had warned Israel and Judah through every prophet and seer: "Turn from your wicked ways! Obey my commands and statutes — the entire law I gave your ancestors, the law I delivered to you through my servants the prophets."

**14** But they refused to listen. They were as stubborn as their ancestors, who had refused to trust the LORD their God.

**15** They rejected his statutes and the covenant he had made with their ancestors, ignoring the warnings he had given them. They chased after empty things and became empty themselves. They imitated the surrounding nations, the very thing the LORD had told them not to do.

**16** They abandoned every command of the LORD their God. They cast two metal calves and set up an Asherah pole. They bowed down to the stars in the sky and worshiped Baal.

**17** They sacrificed their own sons and daughters in the fire, practiced divination and sorcery, and sold themselves to evil in the LORD's sight, provoking his anger.

**18** So the LORD was furious with Israel and banished them from his presence. Only the tribe of Judah remained.

**19** But even Judah failed to keep the LORD's commands. They too adopted the practices Israel had introduced.

**20** The LORD rejected the entire nation of Israel. He punished them and handed them over to raiders, until finally he thrust them from his presence altogether.

**21** When the LORD tore Israel away from the house of David, the people had made Jeroboam son of Nebat their king. Jeroboam led Israel away from following the LORD and drew them into terrible sin.

**22** The Israelites persisted in all the sins Jeroboam had committed. They never turned away from them,

**23** until the LORD finally removed Israel from his presence, just as he had warned through all his servants the prophets. Israel was taken from their homeland into exile in Assyria, where they remain to this day.

**24** The king of Assyria then brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the towns of Samaria to replace the Israelites. These newcomers took over Samaria and occupied its towns.

**25** When they first settled there, they did not worship the LORD. So the LORD sent lions among them, and the lions began killing people.

**26** A report was sent to the king of Assyria: "The peoples you deported and resettled in Samaria do not know the requirements of the god of that land. He has sent lions among them, and the lions are killing them because they don't know what the god of the land requires."

**27** The king of Assyria ordered, "Send back one of the priests you took from there. Have him go live there and teach the people the requirements of the god of the land."

**28** So one of the priests who had been exiled from Samaria went back and settled in Bethel. He began teaching the people how to worship the LORD.

**29** But each national group continued making its own gods and setting them up in the shrines the former inhabitants had built — each group in the towns where they lived.

**30** The people from Babylon made Succoth-benoth; the people from Cuthah made Nergal; the people from Hamath made Ashima;

**31** the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children as sacrifices to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.

**32** They worshiped the LORD too, but they appointed all sorts of their own people as priests at the shrines, and these priests offered sacrifices for them at the local high places.

**33** They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods, following the customs of the nations from which they had come.

**34** They continue these same practices to this day. They do not truly worship the LORD or follow the statutes, rules, laws, and commands that the LORD gave the descendants of Jacob, whom he renamed Israel.

**35** When the LORD made his covenant with them, he commanded: "Do not worship other gods. Do not bow down to them, serve them, or sacrifice to them.

**36** Worship only the LORD, who brought you out of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. Bow down to him alone. Sacrifice to him alone.

**37** Carefully obey the statutes, rules, laws, and commands he wrote for you. Do this always. Do not worship other gods.

**38** Do not forget the covenant I made with you. Do not worship other gods.

**39** Worship the LORD your God alone. He is the one who will rescue you from all your enemies."

**40** But they refused to listen. They kept right on following their old practices.

**41** So these nations worshiped the LORD while simultaneously serving their own idols. Their children did the same, and their grandchildren after them. As their ancestors did, so they continue to do to this day.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verses 7-23 — The narrator's sermon:** This is the theological heart of the entire book of Kings — not just a chapter summary, but the narrator's closing argument for why an entire nation was destroyed. It reads like a courtroom speech: the charge, the evidence, the warnings ignored, the verdict. Every sin from the Deuteronomic code is catalogued. Every prophetic warning is recalled. The conclusion is devastating: "the LORD removed Israel from his presence."

**Verse 15 — "chased after empty things and became empty":** This is one of the Bible's most penetrating psychological observations. The Hebrew says they pursued *hevel* (vapor, breath, nothingness) and *became* hevel. You are shaped by what you worship. Pursue substance, you gain substance. Pursue emptiness, you become empty. This principle echoes through Jeremiah, the Psalms, and into Paul's letter to the Romans.

**Verse 18 — "Only Judah remained":** The narrator drops this like a guillotine blade — and then immediately adds (v.19) that Judah also failed to keep the commands. It is a stay of execution, not an acquittal. The reader already knows where this story ends: in 586 BCE, with Babylon doing to Judah what Assyria did to Israel.

**Verse 25-28 — Lions and syncretism:** There is dark humor in this scene. The Assyrian settlers are attacked by lions. Their diagnosis: "We don't know the local god's requirements." Their solution: import an Israelite priest to teach them. The priest settles in Bethel — ironically, the very place where Jeroboam set up his rival cult. The result is not true YHWH-worship but a grotesque patchwork of YHWH plus every other deity.

**Verse 41 — "to this day":** The chapter ends with a devastating portrait of permanent syncretism. These people "feared the LORD" and "served their idols" — simultaneously and indefinitely. The narrator sees this as a theological impossibility: you cannot fear YHWH and serve other gods. But they do. And their children do. And their grandchildren do. The disease is hereditary.

*— PNEUMA*
